# Repetition Without Repetition
**What it is** — Bernstein's (1967) formulation, and the single most portable idea in the book. Ordinary repetition means rehearsing and reproducing a *technique*. **Repetition without repetition means repeatedly solving the same performance problem, challenged differently each time.** What repeats is the problem; what varies is the solution.
The authors are explicit that repetition itself is not the enemy — "while repetition is an important feature of practice, repetition without repetition is even better." And it can be **turbocharged by adding variability**: running the same task at different fatigue levels, or changing the performance context in a way that meaningfully challenges the player.
**Why it works** — Because no two problems on a field are ever the same, so no two solutions will be either. Practising one movement prepares one problem. Practising the *process* of solving prepares the class of problems. The player is, in the authors' phrase, **learning to learn to move** (Adolph & Hoch, 2019; Harlow, 1949) — the degrees of freedom of perception, cognition and action

# Representative Design
**What it is** — How well a practice task reproduces the *relevant conditions* of the competitive environment it prepares for. The term comes from Egon Brunswik; the sporting insight comes from Gibson's wartime work on pilots, who used information from the environment to judge approach speed, direction, descent timing and position in airspace. If practice does not contain that information, it does not prepare the coupling that uses it.
The book gives three tests. A representative practice task should:
**(a)** include appropriate and pertinent **information sources** for players to use;
**(b)** allow players to **act** — move, adapt and think as they would in competition;
**(c)** set **goals and intentions the players can commit to** (defend with speed, exploit a specific area) rather than a set of general instructions and prescribed movements.

# Affordances Are Opportunities for Action
**What it is** — An **affordance** is an opportunity for action (Gibson, 1979; Fajen et al., 2009) — or, in Withagen et al.'s (2012) framing, an **invitation** in the environment beckoning a player to act in a certain way. Affordances are the openings within a problem that guide and channel how a movement solution organises.
One qualification matters and is routinely lost: **affordances do not cause behaviour.** They constrain or channel it — eliminating options, offering invitations. They describe what this player *can and cannot do* under the constraints of this unfolding problem, in this context.
Gibson's own everyday examples make the shape of the concept clear: a surface that is walk-on-able, a tree that is climb-up-able, a chair that is sit-on-able. On a football field the affordances are less obvious but no less real — a gap that is pass-through-able, a defender that is beat-outside-able.

# External Focus of Attention Beats Internal
**What it is** — Coaching cues fall into two categories (Wulf et al., 1998). An **internal focus** cue directs attention inward, to the movement or position of the body: "bend your knees more," "snap your wrist," "hit it with the inside of your foot." An **external focus** cue directs attention outward, to the effect the movement has on the environment or to something in it: where the ball goes, the position of the safety, the ground being pushed away. From 1998 to 2021 the literature accumulated **73 studies (1,824 participants) showing superior *performance* under external focus, and 40 studies (1,274 participants) showing better *learning*** (Chua et al., 2021). The benefits are durable — still present in retention tests 24 hours later — and they transfer to untrained tasks.
**Why it works** — Attending to your own body interferes with the self-organising control that produces the movement; attending to the outcome lets it organise itself around the goal. Porter et al. **What it is** — The authors' position on programmed speed work: **the majority of sprint work should take the form of contextually-driven movement problems** and the solutions that emerge from them. **What it is** — The chapter written for realism. The authors accept that **tradition runs rampant in football** and that many readers **"won't be ready to go all-in."** So they offer a compromise: minor practical changes that move a learning environment toward the ecological approach without requiring anyone to rebuild practice. All of them are described as **battle tested by the authors with athletes across levels, including NFL and other professional players.**

# Task Simplification Is Not Task Decomposition
**What it is** — The distinction that makes constraints-led practice usable in the real world, and the one most often collapsed. **Task simplification means reducing task difficulty** (Chow et al., 2022) **while keeping the perception-action link intact.** Task decomposition breaks the movement into parts and drills each in isolation ([[framework--three-types-of-task-decomposition]]). Both make things easier. Only one keeps the skill.

# Newell's Model of Interacting Constraints
**What it is** — Karl Newell's (1986) model, the operational heart of the constraints-led approach. Coordination solutions **emerge** under three interacting classes of constraint:
- **Individual (organismic)** — the performer: height, limb length, strength, fatigue, injury status, movement history, intentions, emotional state.
- **Task** — the problem as set: the goal, the rules, the equipment, the space, the number of players, the time available.
- **Environmental** — the surrounding conditions: surface, weather, light, noise, social and cultural context.
**The word means the opposite of what it means in ordinary speech.** In everyday language a constraint is a restriction. In this science, **a constraint is a link — physical or informational — that facilitates, limits, or shapes how a system reorganises over time.** Constraints are not obstacles to be removed; they are the sources of information that shape what emerges. This is the most common point of confusion when the idea is introduced to coaches, and it is worth correcting explicitly every time.

# Repetition Without Repetition
**What it is** — Bernstein's (1967) formulation, and the single most portable idea in the book. Ordinary repetition means rehearsing and reproducing a *technique*. **Repetition without repetition means repeatedly solving the same performance problem, challenged differently each time.** What repeats is the problem; what varies is the solution.

# Representative Design
**What it is** — How well a practice task reproduces the *relevant conditions* of the competitive environment it prepares for. The term comes from Egon Brunswik; the sporting insight comes from Gibson's wartime work on pilots, who used information from the environment to judge approach speed, direction, descent timing and position in airspace. # External Focus of Attention Beats Internal
**What it is** — Coaching cues fall into two categories (Wulf et al., 1998). An **internal focus** cue directs attention inward, to the movement or position of the body: "bend your knees more," "snap your wrist," "hit it with the inside of your foot." # Intensity and Complexity as Two Independent Axes

Individual Differences in Learning a Sports Skill
Miriam Chang Yi Lee1*, Jia Yi Chow1, John Komar2, Clara Wee Keat Tan1, Chris Button3
1 Physical Education and Sports Science, National Institute of Education, Nanyang Technological University, Singapore, Singapore, 2 CETAPS, Faculty of Sports Sciences,
3 School of Physical Education, Sport and Exercise Sciences, University of Otago, Dunedin, New Zealand
Abstract
Learning a sports skill is a complex process in which practitioners are challenged to cater for individual differences. The main
purpose of this study was to explore the effectiveness of a Nonlinear Pedagogy approach for learning a sports skill. Twenty-
four 10-year-old females participated in a 4-week intervention involving either a Nonlinear Pedagogy (i.e.,manipulation of
task constraints including equipment and rules) or a Linear Pedagogy (i.e., prescriptive, repetitive drills) approach to learn a
tennis forehand stroke. Performance accuracy scores, movement criterion scores and kinematic data were measured during
pre-intervention, post-intervention and retention tests. While both groups showed improvements in performance accuracy
scores over time, the Nonlinear Pedagogy group displayed a greater number of movement clusters at post-test indicating
the presence of degeneracy (i.e., many ways to achieve the same outcome). The results suggest that degeneracy is effective
for learning a sports skill facilitated by a Nonlinear Pedagogy approach. These findings challenge the common
misconception that there must be only one ideal movement solution for a task and thus have implications for coaches and
educators when designing instructions for skill acquisition.

Sports Skill. PLoS ONE 9(8): e104744. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0104744

Introduction
Motor skill acquisition during childhood forms the foundation
for lifelong participation in sport, essential for long-term health
and fitness benefits [1]. Learning a sports skill is a complex process
that involves a multitude of factors. At the level of the learner,
every individual is unique with differences in characteristics such
as
genetic
composition,
social-economic
backgrounds,
prior
experiences, and learning styles [2]. A key challenge for movement
practitioners
is
to
cater
for
this
abundance
of
individual
characteristics during practice. Clearly, an instructional approach
underpinned by a robust theoretical framework is essential for
effective acquisition of a sports skill.
Traditionally, practitioners (e.g., coaches, teachers, etc.) have
adopted approaches which are prescriptive and repetitive, utilizing
technical demonstrations that provide learners with a ‘‘visual
template or criterion model’’ for the desired skill [3]. The
underlying assumption that has fuelled such pedagogies is that
an ideal movement pattern exists for a task and that the
practitioner’s role is to help learners to recreate that pattern [3].
Furthermore, some theorists have suggested that learning is a
gradual, linear process offering the ‘power law’ as supportive
evidence [4,5], although this viewpoint is not without its critics [6].
An increasing amount of evidence from the Dynamical Systems
Theory (DST) perspective challenge these traditional assumptions
about skill acquisition [3,7,8].
From the DST viewpoint, the learning process does not
generally follow continuous linear progressions of behaviour but
rather involves sudden discontinuous changes over time [9].
Learners should be conceived as nonlinear dynamical systems,
comprising numerous component parts that interact and self-
organize to form stable patterns. The emergence of self-organized
functional movement solutions is faciliated through the interaction
of performer, task and environment constraints which act as
boundaries to shape goal-directed behaviours. Unlike tradtional
approaches in motor learning, there is no central controller (e.g.,
an authoritative coach) that determines how movement behaviors
should be produced to meet task goals [7]. Chow et al. [10] were
the first to propose the use of the umbrella term ‘‘Nonlinear
Pedagogy’’ to capture how practitioners can benefit from these
contemporary theoretical concepts.
Grounded in the constraints-led approach, Nonlinear Pedagogy
(referred to from here as NP) advocates the manipulation of key
constraints that form boundaries for the learner to explore
functional movement solutions [11,12]. Thus, NP provides a
framework for pedagocial principles that can be used to account
for the nonlinear behavioural changes typically observed in
learning movement skills. It provides a theoretical impetus for
practitioners to incorporate ‘‘representativeness, manipulation of
constraints, attentional focus, functional variability, and the
maintenance of pertinent information-movement couplings’’ to
effectively design motor learning interventions [13]. Firstly, NP

Abstract
Background/Objectives: Differential learning (DL) amplifies natural fluctuations in move-
ment execution and, in its more extreme forms, facilitates repetition-free training with
minimal external feedback. While increasingly recognized in the field of skill acquisition,
its application in anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rehabilitation remains underexplored.
Methods: This study examined the application of DL in the rehabilitation of an 18-year-old
trained basketball player following left-ACL reconstruction. The athlete completed a
42-week rehabilitation program in which DL principles were incorporated throughout the
pre-operative, early, mid-, and late phases, culminating in return to sport. Training included
differential mobility work, motor control, plyometric exercises, and sport-specific drills.
Functional recovery was evaluated using single-leg hop tests, change-of-direction tasks,
and sprint performance, while self-reported knee function was monitored via the Interna-
tional Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) questionnaire. Results: Results indicated
substantial improvements in both functional performance and psychological readiness.
The IKDC score increased from 13.8% at baseline to 95.4% postoperatively, reaching the
normal functional range. An ACL-RSI score of 85.2%, and inter-limb asymmetries were
reduced to below 10%. Strength, agility, and sprint performance exceeded pre-injury levels.
Conclusions: DL again shows potential as an effective approach to facilitating recovery
and return to sport after ACL reconstruction, but larger controlled studies are needed
for validation.
Keywords:
motor learning; neuromuscular; return-to-play; movement variability;
sensorimotor integration; anterior cruciate ligament injury; rehabilitation

sprint performance

Keywords:
Focus of attention
Sprinting
Human performance

a b s t r a c t
Two experiments evaluated the inﬂuence of attentional focus on 10-meter sprint time and
start kinetics in a group of collegiate soccer players and highly experienced sprinters. In
Experiment 1, the collegiate soccer players were asked to perform 10-meter sprints under
an external focus condition, an internal focus condition and a control condition. For the 10-
meter sprint time, the results showed that both the external focus and control conditions
resulted in signiﬁcantly faster sprint times than the internal focus condition. There were no
signiﬁcant differences observed between the external focus and control conditions. There
were also no signiﬁcant differences observed across any of the conditions for a select set
of kinetic variables. In Experiment 2, the highly experienced sprinters performed the same
10-meter sprint task using the same instructional conditions as in Experiment 1. For the
10-meter sprint time and kinetic variables, there were no signiﬁcant differences observed
across any of the conditions. These results provide new evidence that experience level
mediates the inﬂuence of attentional focus on sprint performance.

1. Introduction
Attentional focus has emerged as an important mediator of performance and learning across a diversity of motor skills
(for a review, see Wulf, 2013). Attentional focus is deﬁned by the conscious intent of an individual to direct their attention
towards speciﬁc features of the environment, or to the action-preparation process, in an effort to execute a motor skill with
superior performance (Magill, 2011). Speciﬁcally, an individual can focus internally on their body movements (i.e., movement
process) or externally on the effect their movements have on the environment (i.e., movement outcome) (Wulf, Hoss, & Prinz,
1998). For example, a coach instructing the vertical jump may provide an internal cue by telling an athlete to ‘‘focus on
explosively extending your hips” or provide an external cue by telling an athlete to ‘‘focus on explosively pushing off the
ground.” While the instructions carry the same message (i.e., get off the ground ‘explosively’), the internal cue calls attention
to the body (i.e., hips) and the external cue calls attention to the effect on the environment (i.e., ground).
The need for coaches and clinical practitioners to optimize verbal instruction and cue selection has motivated numerous
investigations into the effects of attentional focus on various motor tasks. The majority of studies evaluating the effects of
attentional focus have found that an external focus of attention results in superior performance and learning compared to

meter sprint time, the results showed that both the external focus and control conditions
resulted in signiﬁcantly faster sprint times than the internal focus condition. There were no
signiﬁcant differences observed between the external focus and control conditions. There
were also no signiﬁcant differences observed across any of the conditions for a select set
of kinetic variables. In Experiment 2, the highly experienced sprinters performed the same
10-meter sprint task using the same instructional conditions as in Experiment 1. For the
10-meter sprint time and kinetic variables, there were no signiﬁcant differences observed
across any of the conditions. These results provide new evidence that experience level
mediates the inﬂuence of attentional focus on sprint performance.

1. Introduction
Attentional focus has emerged as an important mediator of performance and learning across a diversity of motor skills
(for a review, see Wulf, 2013). Attentional focus is deﬁned by the conscious intent of an individual to direct their attention
towards speciﬁc features of the environment, or to the action-preparation process, in an effort to execute a motor skill with
superior performance (Magill, 2011). Speciﬁcally, an individual can focus internally on their body movements (i.e., movement
process) or externally on the effect their movements have on the environment (i.e., movement outcome) (Wulf, Hoss, & Prinz,
1998). For example, a coach instructing the vertical jump may provide an internal cue by telling an athlete to ‘‘focus on
explosively extending your hips” or provide an external cue by telling an athlete to ‘‘focus on explosively pushing off the
ground.” While the instructions carry the same message (i.e., get off the ground ‘explosively’), the internal cue calls attention
to the body (i.e., hips) and the external cue calls attention to the effect on the environment (i.e., ground).
The need for coaches and clinical practitioners to optimize verbal instruction and cue selection has motivated numerous
investigations into the effects of attentional focus on various motor tasks. The majority of studies evaluating the effects of
attentional focus have found that an external focus of attention results in superior performance and learning compared to

How a constraints-led approach can be implemented in American football
Nonlinear pedagogy is a framework based on the theory of ecological 
dynamics that provides principles for practitioners to use in a learner- 
environment-centred approach to teaching and coaching, especially related 
to constraint manipulation. The original constraints model proposed by 
(Newell, 1986) emphasised that movement is an emergent property of three 
interacting constraints, classified into the organism, environment, and task 
categories. Applied to sports through the constraints-led approach (CLA), 
Davids et al. (2008) suggested that task constraints are reflective of impor­
tant variables like game rules, equipment, playing area dimensions, bound­
aries, opponents, and teammates; environmental constraints reflect physical 
properties like ambient light, humidity, temperature, and social expecta­
tions; and organismic (performer) constraints reflect personal properties like 
height, body weight, limb segment lengths, emotions, psychological states, 
and fatigue levels. (Newell, 1986) emphasised that the interaction of con­
straints from these categories shapes behaviours. Next, we expand on what 
these ideas may imply through the presentation of two practical case 
examples from different levels of performance in American football. The 
purpose of these examples is not to provide practitioners with a detailed 
“book of drills” but to exemplify what these ideas may mean for them when 
exploring an ecological dynamics approach.

{"result":[{"page":2,"text":"approach. For example, Sackett’s (1996) seminal evidence-based
medicine model underscores that evidence-based medicine is built
on three requirements: (a) best scientiﬁc evidence; (b) the clin-
ician’s expertise; and (c) the client’s preferences, values, and goals.
For skill acquisition specialists, this means that experience and
expertise of high-performance coaches, coupled with the players’
unique needs and wants, must operate alongside evidence from
skill acquisition science in order to provide a robust platform for the
optimization of skill learning and performance. However, my
recent inspection of the evidence supporting commonly imple-
mented skill acquisition interventions led me to conclude that there
is simply not enough consistent, credible, and high-level evidence
to support the efﬁcacy and effectiveness of skill acquisition inter-
ventions in high-performance sport. I will illustrate these points
through several recently published studies, which are by no means
an exhaustive depiction of this literature.
A recent review by Choo et al. (2024) scoped randomized
controlled trials on typical skill acquisition interventions such as
instruction and demonstration, practice design, perceptual training,
attention, augmented feedback, self-regulation and self-control,
and imagery and mental practice used for the training of sports-
related skills. They found that this body of literature was skewed
toward the examination of golf skills, closed skills practiced in a
highly controlled environment, and relied heavily on the recruit-
ment of inexperienced learners. This raises a key question: How
applicable are the ﬁndings in the skill acquisition literature related
to sports skills to the learning of expert performers in highly
complex, dynamic, and open skill sports?
This scarcity of evidence is not the only barrier to consistently
implementing skill acquisition science in sports practice. There is
also a signiﬁcant issue with the credibility of skill acquisition
research. For example, the outstanding critical work by McKay
et al. (2025) questioned the veracity of evidence supporting self-
controlled or self-regulated practice, the beneﬁcial effects of an
external focus of attention (McKay et al., 2024), and the beneﬁts of
implicit motor learning (McKay & Carter, 2023), many of which
feature prominently in contemporary skill acquisition theories such
as ecological dynamics (e.g., Araújo et al., 2006) or OPTIMAL
(Optimizing Performance through Intrinsic Motivation and Atten-
tion for Learning) theory (e.g., Wulf & Lewthwaite, 2016).
Therefore, it seems that there is at least inconsistent supporting
evidence in the literature for the efﬁcacy and effectiveness of skill
acquisition interventions in high-performance sport. As a result, the
integration of skill acquisition specialists who are tasked with using
the skill acquisition literature to optimize performance and learning
—without more robust, high-level evidence to support their prac-
tices—is surely putting the cart before the horse.
Argument 2: Skill Acquisition Specialists
Compete With Coaches’ Skill Acquisition
Expertise
Many experienced coaches already embody the principles and
practices central to skill acquisition science, sometimes through
formal education but often through decades of honed coaching
intuition. This makes sense, as the very essence of effective
coaching aligns seamlessly with the objectives of skill acquisition,
and many coaches were doing this well before skill acquisition
specialists made their appearance. Steel et al. (2013) highlighted
this overlap when they asked ﬁve coaches and ﬁve athletes about

SPEED BUT NOT DEFENSIVE AGILITY IN AUSTRALIAN
RULES FOOTBALL
WARREN B. YOUNG, IAN R. MILLER, AND SCOTT W. TALPEY
Faculty of Health, Federation University Australia, Ballarat, Australia
ABSTRACT
Young, WB, Miller, IR, and Talpey, SW. Physical qualities
predict change-of-direction speed but not defensive agility in
Australian Rules football. J Strength Cond Res 29(1): 206–
212, 2015—The purpose of this study was to determine the
relationships between selected physical qualities, change-of-
direction (COD) speed, and defensive agility performance in
Australian Rules football players. Twenty-four male community-
level players were assessed on sprint acceleration (10-m time),
maximum strength (3 repetition-maximum half squat), leg
power (countermovement jump), reactive strength (drop jump),
and a single COD speed test and a defensive agility test.
Change-of-direction
speed
was
correlated
with
reactive
strength (r = 20.645, p = 0.001) and sprint acceleration
(r = 0.510, p = 0.011). Multiple regression indicated that
the combined physical qualities explained 56.7% of the vari-
ance associated with COD speed (adjusted R2 = 0.567, p #
0.05). Participants were median split into faster and slower
COD speed groups, and these were compared by indepen-
dent t-tests. The faster group was signiﬁcantly better (p #
0.05) on the sprint acceleration and reactive strength tests
(large effect size). The correlations between physical qualities
and agility were trivial to small (r = 20.101 to 0.123, p . 0.05)
and collectively explained only 14.2% of the variance associ-
ated with agility performance (adjusted R2 = 20.142, p .
0.05). When faster and slower agility groups were compared,
there were trivial to moderate differences (p . 0.05) in all
physical qualities. It was concluded that reactive strength
and sprint acceleration are important for COD speed, but the
physical qualities assessed are not associated with defensive
agility performance. For agility tasks similar to those in this
study, sprint and resistance training should not be emphasized,
and training other factors, such as the development of sport-
speciﬁc technique and cognitive skill, is recommended.
KEY WORDS evasion sports, side step, sprint acceleration,
decision making
INTRODUCTION
I
n many invasion sports, such as the various codes of
football, agility is an important quality. If an attacking
player can evade defenders, the ball can be moved for-
ward to provide scoring opportunities. Conversely,
defensive agility is required to block attacking movements,
and to increase pressure on the attacker with the objective
of causing a turnover. Agility has been deﬁned as a change in
speed or direction in response to a stimulus (23). For example,
in football codes, defensive agility involves either a change in
speed, change in direction, or both, and is always in reaction
to the attacker’s movements. Despite this, most training, test-
ing of athletes, and research concerned with agility involve
preplanned change-of-direction (COD) movements around
obstacles such as poles and cones (1,11,12). Such activities
can be described as COD speed rather than as agility (3,33),
and generally do not occur during competition.
Considerable research has been conducted to determine
the relative importance of ﬁtness components such as speed,
strength, and power to COD speed. For example, various
measures of explosive leg muscle function have been
reported to have statistically signiﬁcant (p # 0.05) correla-
tions with different tests of COD speed (16,17,28,33). A drop
jump (DJ) test proposed to assess explosive leg extensor
function in a fast stretch-shortening cycle (reactive strength)
correlated more strongly with COD speed than a test of
concentric-only leg power did (33). The authors suggested
the stronger correlation was because of the similarity in the
leg push-off mechanism in the DJ and COD tests. Further,
training that causes gains in leg power has been shown to
transfer to improved COD speed (13,15), although this has
not always been found (27).
Unfortunately, there is a paucity of research examining the
relationship between physical qualities and agility perfor-
mance. Henry et al. (8) recently reported correlation coefﬁ-
cients ,0.3 (p . 0.05) between an agility test (with reaction)

return to sport in elite football - Part 1: Load planning
M. Taberner a, b, *, T. Allen c, d, J. O'keefe e, D.D. Cohen f, g

28 October 2021

Keywords:
Elite football
Return to sport
‘Control-chaos continnum’
Contextual factors
a b s t r a c t
The ‘control-chaos continnum’ is an adaptable framework developed to guide the on-pitch rehabilitation
process in elite football. One of the key objectives of the continuum is to progressively return players to
their preinjury chronic running load, while incorporating the qualitative aspects of movement and
cognitive stresses integral to competitive match-play. Whilst injury and player-speciﬁc considerations
are key to an individualised rehabilitation approach, a host of contextual factors also play an important
role in return to sport (RTS) planning. In this article, we highlight some key intrinsic and extrinsic
contextual factors for the practitioner to consider in the RTS planning process to help mitigate reinjury
risk upon a return to team training. While a return to chronic running load is generally a critical
component of the framework, we highlight circumstances in elite football where it is a less relevant
factor in RTS decision-making.

1. Introduction
The ‘control-chaos continuum’ (CCC), is an adaptable framework
for on-pitch rehabilitation in elite football (Taberner et al., 2019a).
The CCC moves from ‘high control’, a base of general training to
‘high chaos’, football-speciﬁc training manipulating constraints to
shape the on-pitch environment to the goals of the practitioner and
injury case (Taberner et al., 2019a; Taberner, 2020). A key compo-
nent of this framework is the safe and effective return of players to
their preinjury chronic running load, whilst progressively incor-
porating the qualitative aspects of movement, football-speciﬁc
skills and cognitive stresses integral to competitive match-play
(Figs. 1 and 2) (Taberner, 2020; Taberner et al., 2019a). The quali-
tative aspects of load have however received less attention in the
literature. These are critical in helping to develop player conﬁdence
and prepare the player for the contextual elements of game-related
movements, such as responses to the movement and speed of the
ball and/or other players before returning to team training/
competition (Jimenez-Rubio et al., 2019, 2021; Taberner, 2020;
Taberner & Cohen, 2018; Taberner et al., 2019b, 2020a, 2020b).
Several case reports describe the application of the CCC each
with their own unique contextual considerations, demonstrating
the use of the framework in preparing players for the crucial return
to competitive match-play (Taberner & Cohen, 2018; Taberner
et al., 2019b, 2020a, 2020b). In these case reports, preinjury
global positioning systems (GPS) data informed planning of
running load progression and the estimation of chronic load tar-
gets. These targets are important to consider in the RTS decision-
making process, as higher rehabilitation loads have been shown
to mitigate against subsequent injury following RTS (Stares et al.,
2018). Despite not being part of current RTS decision-making
models (Shrier, 2015), determining and achieving chronic load ca-
pacity is an important component of the rehabilitation pathway
and RTS decision-making (Allen, Wilson, Cohen, & Taberner, 2021;
Blanch & Gabbett, 2016; Taberner & Cohen, 2018; Taberner et al.,
2019b, 2020a, 2020b).
* Corresponding author. Performance and Medical Department, Orlando Magic
Basketball Club, Orlando, USA.

The value of opposed and unopposed practice: An ecological 
dynamics rationale for skill development
Tom E. Parry
a, Shawn Myszka
b, Tyler Yearby
b, Mark O Sullivan
c, 
and Fabian Otte
d
aKinesiology Program, Butler University, Indianapolis, Indiana, USA; bEmergence, Minneapolis, Minnesota, USA; 
cDepartment of Sport and Social Sciences, Norwegian School of Sport Sciences, Oslo, Norway; dIndependent 
researcher
ABSTRACT
Recently, there has been a great deal of progress in our under­
standing of skill learning and the types of practice activities that 
best develop athletes. Evidence suggests sport practitioners’ 
assumptions about learning dramatically influence the types of 
practice activities they employ. Historically, dominant theoretical 
approaches emphasize a strong focus on repeated practice to 
“acquire” technical skills before these movements are applied in 
dynamic games. Moreover, these approaches to skill acquisition 
overvalue the importance of repetition of ideal movement pat­
terns. Contemporary theories, such as ecological dynamics, suggest 
that movement problem-solving in alive environments, which 
involves opposed practice, is more beneficial for skill development. 
This paper explored the theoretical and practical differences in the 
rationale for opposed and unopposed practice tasks from an eco­
logical dynamics lens. Example practice activities, underpinned by 
ecological dynamics, will be presented as alternate activities for 
common isolated technical drills.
KEYWORDS 
Coaching; sport; motor skill 
learning; practice design; 
ecological dynamics
“In human behaviour the act of ‘doing’ never occurs in a vacuum. To do is always to do 
something somewhere” (Araújo & Davids, 2009, p. 6). Ultimately, context is key (Otte et al., 
2021). This identifies an important question for coaches: How should practice be structured 
to effectively support the learning and transfer of sport skills to the competitive context? 
(Roca & Ford, 2020). Determining whether a drill or practice activity is effective needs to be 
considered in relation to transfer to competition (Parry & O’Rourke, 2023). Therefore, it 
could be suggested that task designs that are unpredictable in nature and encourage athletes 
to act in relation to information that simulates aspects of the competitive environment will 
best support transfer (Davids et al., 2013). With this in mind, it is worth considering the 
ongoing debate within coaching circles about the efficacy of opposed and unopposed 
practice tasks on the development of skilled behavior in sport.
It has been highlighted that isolated, unopposed technical drills are prevalent across a 
number of different sports at all levels, from elite to recreational (Gearing & Bridge, 2024; 
Partington & Cushion, 2013; Roca & Ford, 2020). How these movements and skills transfer 
to competition needs to be a primary concern for coaches. Pill (2013) defined isolated skill

34:- "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data" — a test's validity doesn't rescue it if it can't be collected consistently at scale. **Explicit** [2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md]
62:- Change of direction is not tested in most sports. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q13): "If the data is captured, it's on an individual sport basis and that information lives with that coach." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q13)**
68:- The Baylor Sport Assessment Table (V4) assigns a specific battery per sport (movement screen, anthropometrics, CMJ, broad jump, weighted throw, upper/lower strength estimation, strength endurance, aerobic fitness, repeat sprint ability, linear sprint, change of direction) rather than testing every sport the same way. **Legacy (interview 2026-09-28, Q9)**; was Inferred. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q9): "That assessment schedule was never used." Inference: the table was never practice, not just outdated. [update-baylor-sport-assessment-table-v4.md]
91:## Speed and sprint
93:- Linear sprint testing uses a 2-point start for team-sport athletes (for reliability), athlete self-selected start timing, at least two maximal-effort reps over 30-40 meters. **Legacy (interview 2026-09-28, Q8)**; was Inferred (author uncertain) [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md]
94:- Split times are interpreted by physical quality, not just total time: 0-10m is read as an acceleration score (reflecting maximal strength/power/slow stretch-shortening-cycle development), 30-40m as a speed score (reflecting sprint-specific/fast stretch-shortening-cycle development), and 40m peak velocity is derived from the 30-40m split divided by 10. **Legacy (interview 2026-09-28, Q8)**; was Inferred (author uncertain) [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md]
95:- SmartSpeed timing gates are the standard tool for sprint, agility, and reaction-time testing across the department. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.7]
97:- Issurin's residual training effects (speed fades fastest, 5 ± 3 days; Block Periodization PDF p. 35, as cited in `docs/synthesis/peaking-and-taper-in-season-football.md`) drive speed programming. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q16): "I believe Issurin. It drives our speed programming in the off-season and what drives sprinting recommendations in season." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q16)** See the residual-effects bullets under Conditioning and Periodization, and Tension 11.
104:- Training time is deliberately weighted toward high motor-unit-recruitment core/ballistic movements (squats, cleans, jumps, throws, sprints); single-joint assistance work is kept to a small share of total volume. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.13; week1-lecture.md p.31]
105:- Off-season strength work prioritizes relative strength and technique first; already-strong athletes shift more time toward strength-speed/speed-strength work. In-season, the stated rule is "maintain intensity, reduce volume" rather than trying to build strength while managing a full competition schedule. **Inferred (transcript + shared slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.20-21; hhpr-5355-class-8-2026.md p.21] Not claimed in the interview. The in-season dose itself is unknown: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q18): "I don't have the specific sets and reps."
114:- All three energy systems (alactic ~10-12s highest power, glycolytic/anaerobic-lactic ~60-90s medium capacity, aerobic hours-long lowest power/highest capacity) are always active simultaneously; programming targets the adaptation, not the drill label. **Explicit** [week3-lecture.md p.19; class-4-2026.md p.15]
122:- "Everything we do is some form of conditioning": lifting, agility work, and skill drills each load a specific energy system (power vs. capacity, alactic/glycolytic/aerobic) and should be classified and counted as conditioning, not treated as separate from it. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md p.31, tables pp.35-42]
152:- Recovery appears in the department's own subcategory list of Athletic Performance (alongside strength, conditioning, speed, agility, power, nutrition, applied performance, sports psychology, RTP), but no specific recovery protocol, sleep target, or monitoring tool is described anywhere in this corpus. **Explicit (named as a subcategory) / gap (no protocol stated)** [week1-lecture.md p.11]
170:- Constraints-led and external-cue coaching are not part of Eric's practice. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q25): "I don't apply it, as I don't fully understand it. I want to know more." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q25)** A learning request, a candidate for a primer.
171:- New movement patterns are expected to take roughly 3-4 weeks of practice to become efficient and low-energy-cost, which informs how much proficiency to expect when a new exercise or drill is introduced. **Inferred (transcript)** [2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md pp.6-7]
202:- HHPR 5355 ("Power, Speed, Agility, & Periodization in Training") is Eric's own graduate-level course, co-taught with Chris Ruf and Michael Wenger; grading is split across two exams (10% and 20%), a group training-plan project (20%), and lecture/lab participation (40%), with a practical (teach-back) component on exams. **Inferred (transcript, syllabus content)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.1]
233:5. **Testing cueing instructions conflict across two protocol documents for the same test.** The Assessment Manual's CMJ instructions say explicitly: "Do not coach the strategy of jumping." The current Force Plate Testing V3 protocol gives testers specific verbal cues to give athletes during CMJ, squat-jump, and hop-test administration ("keep chest up," "land softly," "land stiff-legged on only the toes"). These may be reconcilable (safety/technique cues vs. jump-strategy cues are different things), but the two documents read differently on how much a tester should say out loud.
234:   **Status (interview 2026-09-28): resolved by Q8.** Inference: with V12 not current, the Force Plate Testing V3 cues govern. Eric did not address the cueing question itself.

- **Bobrownicki, R., Carson, H. J., MacPherson, A. C., et al. (2022).** Constraints of the constraints-led approach in American football and comments on Yearby et al. (2022). *Sports Coaching Review, 15*(1), 46–58. [doi:10.1080/21640629.2022.2158579](https://doi.org/10.1080/21640629.2022.2158579) · [Edinburgh Research Explorer](https://www.research.ed.ac.uk/en/publications/constraints-of-the-constraints-led-approach-in-american-football-/)
  **A direct, peer-reviewed rebuttal to this course's anchor paper (`7M8YQMKU`), in this exact sport, in the same journal.** The authors (University of Edinburgh) accept the CLA is a useful tool but argue that **as a standalone approach it carries mechanistic and epistemological problems that block experimental comparison and limit its novelty and real-world applicability**, and that drawing on a **wider set of theoretical perspectives** serves practitioners better.
  **This supersedes Fransen (`CBJGJQX5`) as the rebuttal to teach.** Fransen argues against skill-acquisition specialists in general; **this argues against this specific paper, about this specific sport.** **Teach the anchor paper and this together, in the same lesson.** A practitioner who has only heard the case *for* folds the first time a physician or coordinator pushes back — and the pushback he meets will look like this one.
  **Related:** *The adaptable coach — a critical review of the practical implications for traditional and constraints-led approaches in sport coaching* ([ResearchGate](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/379382191)) — a second critical review, not yet assessed.

### The anchor paper is free

- **The Version of Record of Yearby et al. is openly available** at Sheffield Hallam's repository: [shura.shu.ac.uk/30272](https://shura.shu.ac.uk/30272/1/Davids-ApplyingEcologicalApproach%28VoR%29.pdf). **Joe can read the anchor paper without a paywall or a library login.** Also on [Academia.edu](https://www.academia.edu/78122686/) and [ResearchGate](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/359706952).

### Shawn Myszka — the credentials this file previously understated

Recorded because the practitioners section describes him only as "movement-skill acquisition with NFL players."
**Performance advisor and movement/skill-acquisition specialist to individual NFL players since 2008 — among the first in the United States to apply an ecological approach in American football.** **Over 145 professional football players, including 7 All-Pro selections and 14 Pro Bowl selections.** Pro Performance Director at **Explosive Edge Athletics** (Minneapolis); **co-director of education at Emergence**; advises **a dozen-plus NFL players a year**. Coined the **Movement Problem-Solving Paradigm**. On X as [@MovementMiyagi](https://x.com/movementmiyagi).

# Primer: the constraints-led approach (CLA)

Written 2026-09-28 for Eric Rash, in answer to the method interview, Q25:
"I don't apply it, as I don't fully understand it. I want to know more."
(`docs/interview/2026-09-28-method-interview.md`, line 167.)

## How to read this

- Source authors' statements are plain text, with a citation.
- **Eric's baseline:** is what `docs/method-baseline.md` or the interview records.
- **Inference:** is my reasoning, not any source's.
- Citation keys:
  - `[Zotero: KEY, PDF p. N]` is a page I read through the Zotero bridge today. PDF page and printed page differ, so I give both where I know them.
  - `[[vault entry]]` is a SecondBrain library entry, with its confidence tag.
  - Myszka, Yearby & Gray (2025), *Enhancing Skill in American Football*, is cited by chapter and the chapter's page range from the vault's contents map (`skill-acquisition/enhancing-skill--myszka/_book.md`). The vault entries carry the chapter, not the page. Nothing here is tagged "confirmed in PDF".
  - **External:** means it is not in Zotero or the vault.

### Why this matters now: the RTP course

`RTP_Constraints_Course` teaches CLA to Joe Smith, assistant athletic trainer. Its subject is the last phase of return to performance in football. Eric is the course's sponsor, not its learner (`RTP_Constraints_Course/CLAUDE.md`). Two of eight lessons are built. Lesson 0003, "the three constraint classes", is next (`docs/STATUS.md` there). Joe's offline package rewrites every "ask the agent" as "ask Eric" (same STATUS, Gotchas).

Inference: so the gap in Q25 is not about the course being wrong. When Joe gets stuck, he is sent to Eric, and Eric has said he does not yet own the ideas. This primer is sized to close that gap: enough to answer Joe's questions and to decide where CLA belongs in Baylor's RTP templates.

## 1. CLA in one paragraph, then the core ideas

A skilled movement is not a stored program replayed on demand. It **emerges** from the athlete, the task and the environment meeting in the moment. So the coach's main tool is the design of the problem, not verbal correction of the movement. The coach changes the problem (space, rules, opponent, targets, time) so that the solution they want becomes the one the athlete is likely to find. CLA is the practical method. Ecological dynamics is the theory under it. Nonlinear pedagogy is the teaching framework that joins them. (Yearby et al. 2024 [Zotero: 7M8YQMKU, PDF p. 11, printed p. 371]; [[framework--nonlinear-pedagogy-and-constraint-classes]] [proven], Myszka ch. 5, pp. 111-132.)

- **Newell's constraints (1986).** Three interacting classes:
  - *Performer:* height, strength, fatigue, injury status, emotion, intention.
  - *Task:* goal, rules, equipment, space, number of players, opponents.
  - *Environment:* surface, light, noise, social context.

  In this field a "constraint" is not a restriction. It is anything that shapes how the movement organises. (Yearby et al. 2024 [Zotero: 7M8YQMKU, PDF p. 11]; [[framework--newell-interacting-constraints]] [proven], Myszka ch. 2, pp. 37-62.)
- **Ecological dynamics.** Skill is a coupling between perception and action. The athlete picks up information, such as a closing defender, and that information regulates the movement. Remove the information and the coupling cannot be practised. ([[principle--representative-design]] [proven], Myszka ch. 2.)
- **Affordance.** An opportunity for action, relative to this athlete: a gap that is pass-through-able, or a defender who can be beaten outside. Affordances do not cause behaviour. - *Reintegration (Blocks 4.1-4.2):* "advance agility (linear + lateral), introduce cutting drills", "reactive agility", then non-contact practice. Inference: this is where CLA fits most naturally. The template says "reactive" but does not define it. The RTP course's lesson 5 plan warns that a coach's hand signal is still an unopposed cue (`RTP_Constraints_Course/reference/course-map.html`). A defined ladder would go: pre-planned, then generic signal, then a live opponent with a simplified task (fewer players, smaller space, a passive then an active defender), then a full opponent.

1. **Evaluation phase.** Should the LE and UE Evaluation milestones gain one opposed, position-specific exposure beside the 10-yard sprint and 5-10-5, or do you want those to stay pure capacity tests, with agility judged by the sport coach in practice?
2. **Where the line sits.** In Baylor's week, which work is capacity (weight room, timed sprints, where CLA mostly does not apply) and which is skill (Reintegration drills, in-season speed exposures)? Who owns the skill side: Athletic Performance, Athletic Medicine, or the sport coach?
3. **Cues.** Do you want the Force Plate V3 internal cues ("keep chest up", "land softly") rewritten as external cues? Or should testing cues stay fixed for reliability, with the external-cue principle kept to training?

# Primer: the constraints-led approach (CLA)

Written 2026-09-28 for Eric Rash, in answer to the method interview, Q25:
"I don't apply it, as I don't fully understand it. I want to know more."
(`docs/interview/2026-09-28-method-interview.md`, line 167.)

## How to read this

- Source authors' statements are plain text, with a citation.
- **Eric's baseline:** is what `docs/method-baseline.md` or the interview records.
- **Inference:** is my reasoning, not any source's.
- Citation keys:
  - `[Zotero: KEY, PDF p. N]` is a page I read through the Zotero bridge today. PDF page and printed page differ, so I give both where I know them.
  - `[[vault entry]]` is a SecondBrain library entry, with its confidence tag.
  - Myszka, Yearby & Gray (2025), *Enhancing Skill in American Football*, is cited by chapter and the chapter's page range from the vault's contents map (`skill-acquisition/enhancing-skill--myszka/_book.md`). The vault entries carry the chapter, not the page. Nothing here is tagged "confirmed in PDF".
  - **External:** means it is not in Zotero or the vault.

### Why this matters now: the RTP course

`RTP_Constraints_Course` teaches CLA to Joe Smith, assistant athletic trainer. Its subject is the last phase of return to performance in football. Eric is the course's sponsor, not its learner (`RTP_Constraints_Course/CLAUDE.md`). Two of eight lessons are built. Lesson 0003, "the three constraint classes", is next (`docs/STATUS.md` there). Joe's offline package rewrites every "ask the agent" as "ask Eric" (same STATUS, Gotchas).

Inference: so the gap in Q25 is not about the course being wrong. When Joe gets stuck, he is sent to Eric, and Eric has said he does not yet own the ideas. This primer is sized to close that gap: enough to answer Joe's questions and to decide where CLA belongs in Baylor's RTP templates.

## 1. CLA in one paragraph, then the core ideas

A skilled movement is not a stored program replayed on demand. It **emerges** from the athlete, the task and the environment meeting in the moment. So the coach's main tool is the design of the problem, not verbal correction of the movement. The coach changes the problem (space, rules, opponent, targets, time) so that the solution they want becomes the one the athlete is likely to find. CLA is the practical method. Ecological dynamics is the theory under it. Nonlinear pedagogy is the teaching framework that joins them. (Yearby et al. 2024 [Zotero: 7M8YQMKU, PDF p. 11, printed p. 371]; [[framework--nonlinear-pedagogy-and-constraint-classes]] [proven], Myszka ch. 5, pp. 111-132.)

- **Newell's constraints (1986).** Three interacting classes:
  - *Performer:* height, strength, fatigue, injury status, emotion, intention.
  - *Task:* goal, rules, equipment, space, number of players, opponents.
  - *Environment:* surface, light, noise, social context.

  In this field a "constraint" is not a restriction. It is anything that shapes how the movement organises. (Yearby et al. 2024 [Zotero: 7M8YQMKU, PDF p. 11]; [[framework--newell-interacting-constraints]] [proven], Myszka ch. 2, pp. 37-62.)
- **Ecological dynamics.** Skill is a coupling between perception and action. The athlete picks up information, such as a closing defender, and that information regulates the movement. Remove the information and the coupling cannot be practised. ([[principle--representative-design]] [proven], Myszka ch. 2.)
- **Affordance.** An opportunity for action, relative to this athlete: a gap that is pass-through-able, or a defender who can be beaten outside. Affordances do not cause behaviour. They invite it or channel it. Fear works the same way, as an affordance to avoid. That matters in RTP. ([[principle--affordances-are-opportunities-for-action]] [proven], Myszka ch. 3, pp. 63-76; [[principle--rate-limiters-and-fear]] [supported], Myszka ch. 9, pp. 209-220.)
- **Self-organisation.** No central controller, whether a coach or a motor program, dictates the pattern. It settles under the constraints. (Lee et al. 2014 [Zotero: XZ8KI5V7, PDF p. 2].)
- **Representative learning design.** A drill is judged by how well it keeps the information and action options of the game. Myszka's three tests:
  - it contains the information players use;
  - it lets them act as they would in a game;
  - it sets a goal they can commit to, not a prescribed movement.

  ([[principle--representative-design]] [proven], Myszka ch. 2.)
- **Degeneracy.** Many movement patterns reach the same outcome. (Lee et al. 2014 [Zotero: XZ8KI5V7, PDF p. 2].)
- **Repetition without repetition (Bernstein 1967).** Repeat the *problem* and let the solution vary, instead of repeating one technique. Bernstein is cited through Yearby et al. 2024 [Zotero: 7M8YQMKU, PDF p. 11] and Myszka ch. 2 ([[principle--repetition-without-repetition]] [proven]). I have not read Bernstein.
- **Variability.** Variability adds difficulty, and its effect on learning is U-shaped. Too little and there is nothing to learn from. Too much and performance collapses. ([[principle--challenge-point-and-practice-variability]], Myszka.) Differential learning (Schöllhorn) is the extreme form: it deliberately adds fluctuation so that no two reps are alike. (Arede et al. 2025 [Zotero: 2MPW3ZQ3, PDF p. 1].)
- **Nonlinear pedagogy.** Four principles, used together:
  - representative design;
  - task simplification;
  - functional variability;
  - manipulation of constraints.

  *Simplify* means make the task easier and keep the opponent. It is the opposite of *decompose*, which means drilling parts in isolation. ([[principle--task-simplification-not-decomposition]] [proven], Myszka ch. 5.)

## 2. How it differs from what Baylor does now

**Eric's baseline:** constraints-led and external-cue coaching are not part of the practice (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 170). Speed testing is closed and timed: 30-40 m, two-point start, splits read as physical qualities (lines 93-94). Change of direction is not tested in most sports (line 62, Q13). The Force Plate Testing V3 protocol gives internal, body-part cues such as "keep chest up" and "land softly" (line 233).

**Drill-and-cue versus design.** The traditional model looks like this. Demonstrate an ideal pattern. Rehearse it unopposed. Correct it with verbal cues. Then add it back into games. Parry et al. (2025) argue that this model "overvalue[s] the importance of repetition of ideal movement patterns". They propose opposed "alive" problems as the better route to transfer [Zotero: CA2CRR6Z, PDF p. 2]. This is a theory paper, not a trial.

**Internal versus external focus (Wulf).**
- An internal cue points at the body ("extend your hips").
- An external cue points at the effect ("push the ground away").

Myszka ch. 1 (pp. 15-36) reports a 2021 meta-analysis by Chua et al.: 73 studies (1,824 participants) favour external focus for performance, and 40 studies (1,274 participants) favour it for learning ([[principle--external-focus-of-attention]] [proven]). The Zotero record for Chua has no full text, so these numbers are second-hand.

Two things temper that result.
- **Experience changes it.** In collegiate soccer players, external focus and control were both faster than internal focus over 10 m. In highly experienced sprinters, the three conditions did not differ (Winkelman et al. 2017 [Zotero: WENT2642, PDF p. 2, printed p. 84]).
- **Its credibility is questioned.** Fransen (2026) cites a 2024 re-examination by McKay et al. of the external-focus evidence [Zotero: CBJGJQX5, PDF p. 2]. I have not read McKay.

Note that Wulf's external focus is a *cueing* theory (OPTIMAL). CLA is a *design* theory. They agree on the practice, so point attention outside the body, but they are different schools. CLA's stronger version is to put the target or opponent in the drill so no cue is needed. (RTP course lesson 0002 learning record, "the opponent does the cueing".)

**Where the evidence is strong and where it is thin**
- *Stronger:* external focus beats internal focus for novices and intermediates, across many small studies (Chua via Myszka ch. 1). Pre-planned COD and reactive agility are different qualities. In 24 community-level Australian football players, physical qualities explained 56.7% of the variance in COD speed but only 14.2% in defensive agility (Young et al. 2015 [Zotero: T4HB866Z, PDF p. 2, printed p. 206]).
- *Thin:* direct trials of CLA and nonlinear pedagogy. The anchor study had 24 ten-year-old girls learning a tennis forehand for 4 weeks. Both groups improved accuracy. The nonlinear group showed more movement solutions, not better outcomes (Lee et al. 2014 [Zotero: XZ8KI5V7, PDF p. 2]). Choo et al. (2024) scoped the randomised trials on skill interventions. The trials were skewed toward golf, closed skills and inexperienced learners (cited in Fransen 2026 [Zotero: CBJGJQX5, PDF p. 2]; Choo not read). No trial I found tests CLA in collegiate football or in RTP. The football papers are case examples (Yearby et al. 2024) and a book (Myszka 2025).

Inference: CLA is well argued and plausible, and its strongest *measured* support comes from neighbouring findings (focus, agility versus COD), not from CLA trials.

## 3. What CLA looks like in Athletic Performance and RTP

**Sprint and change of direction.** Myszka's position is that most sprint work should appear as an affordance: a player chased from behind, not a sprint run for its own sake ([[heuristic--contextual-sprint-work]] [untested], Myszka ch. 8, pp. 195-208).

Moyer (SCN sprint course, lesson 10) offers a middle route that fits a speed program better. For a technique change, go *isolate* (straight line, full attention, speed ramped by self-rated effort), then *integrate* (one added stimulus at a time: head turned, holding a ball, chased in a line), then *improvise* (zig-zag chases, small-sided games). At the improvise stage he switches to constraints-led and differential-learning methods. If a new stimulus brings the old pattern back, step back a stage ([[framework--isolate-integrate-improvise-sprint-technique]] [contested]). His favourite "cue" is a wicket: a task constraint that does the coaching ([[heuristic--sprint-cue-selection-test-outcome-and-feel]] [contested], lesson 9 and Live 2).

**RTP templates** (`staging/rtp/Baylor LE Rehab Program Template.md`, lines 8-9 and 39-50; UE template lines 8-9 and 38-48)
- *Reintegration (Blocks 4.1-4.2):* "advance agility (linear + lateral), introduce cutting drills", "reactive agility", then non-contact practice. Inference: this is where CLA fits most naturally. The template says "reactive" but does not define it. The RTP course's lesson 5 plan warns that a coach's hand signal is still an unopposed cue (`RTP_Constraints_Course/reference/course-map.html`). A defined ladder would go: pre-planned, then generic signal, then a live opponent with a simplified task (fewer players, smaller space, a passive then an active defender), then a full opponent.
- *Evaluation (Block 5):* the milestones are SLJ, 10-yard sprint, 5-10-5 and 100% workload. Inference: all three tests are pre-planned. Given Young et al. 2015, they certify COD *speed* and capacity, not agility. Myszka makes the same point: action capacity is not skill ([[principle--action-capacity-is-not-skill]] [proven], ch. 1). One opposed, position-specific exposure, scored on the outcome of the problem, would close that gap. It would not replace the tests.
- *UE template:* the throwing progression is velocity and distance. Inference: the CLA addition is throws against a live read (a moving receiver or a pass rusher's timing) before full practice.
- *Dosing:* Harries treats intensity and complexity as two separate axes. A late-stage drill can stay controlled if its speed is still climbing, while an action that is already at speed can go into chaos sooner ([[framework--intensity-complexity-two-independent-axes]] [supported], Part 2, ~04:48-09:47). He also steps practice structure from block to serial to random across the levels ([[framework--practice-structure-block-serial-random-by-level]] [contested], Part 5, ~04:03-07:26, Part-5.pdf pp. 2-3). Taberner's control-chaos continuum runs from general training to football-specific training that manipulates constraints, alongside a return to pre-injury chronic running load (Taberner et al. 2022 [Zotero: SK32YKG2, PDF p. 1, printed p. 67]).

**Weight room: where CLA applies less.** Inference: a squat or a clean has no opponent and no information to perceive. Its goal is capacity, which Myszka classes as a performer constraint, not skill (ch. 1). CLA ideas that still fit there: external cues, and task constraints such as a target height or a bar-speed band instead of a body-part cue. One naming trap: Moir et al. (2018) use "constraints-led" for the *mechanical* limits on sprinting, such as stance time and force direction, to guide resistance-training choices [Zotero: G5X9J23E, PDF p. 1, printed p. 47]. That is a different use of the word from Newell's model.

All of these are Inference, built from the sources cited.

2. **When** I would cue a body part in a sprint or jump, **I** swap it for an external cue or a task constraint (wicket, target, chaser), **because** external focus is at least as good for non-experts (Winkelman 2017, PDF p. 2). 2. **When** I would cue a body part in a sprint or jump, **I** swap it for an external cue or a task constraint (wicket, target, chaser), **because** external focus is at least as good for non-experts (Winkelman 2017, PDF p. 2). Moyer keeps an internal cue only if it tests better on the clock (lesson 9).

3. **When** a returning athlete fails a reactive drill, **I** simplify it (passive defender, more space, fewer options) and do not decompose it into cone work, **because** decomposition removes the information the drill is meant to train ([[principle--task-simplification-not-decomposition]]).

4. **When** a drill runs the same rep more than about 10 times, **I** keep the goal and change one constraint per rep (start position, angle, defender timing), **because** repetition without repetition trains the problem, not one solution (Myszka ch. 2).

lines: ## 5. Critiques and limits

- **"Useful tool, not a whole approach."** Bobrownicki et al. responded directly to the football anchor paper. They accept CLA as "a useful tool" but argue that "ecological approaches alone are insufficient to address the complexity and diversity of real-world sporting contexts". They call for "pragmatic balance" within the coach's professional judgement. **External:** Bobrownicki, Carson, MacPherson & Collins, *Sports Coaching Review* 15(1): 46-58, doi:10.1080/21640629.2022.2158579, abstract read from the Edinburgh repository. The paper is not in Zotero. It is the planned anchor for the RTP course's lesson 8.

-- **Evidence quality.** Fransen (2026) concludes there is "not enough consistent, credible, and high-level evidence" for skill-acquisition interventions in high-performance sport [Zotero: CBJGJQX5, PDF p. 2]. He also names "confusing, not convincing, language" as a barrier (same page).

+- **Evidence quality.** Fransen (2026) concludes there is "not enough consistent, credible, and high-level evidence" for skill-acquisition interventions in high-performance sport [Zotero: CBJGJQX5, PDF p. 2]. He also names the field's language as a barrier: "confusing" rather than "convincing" (same page).

- **Theory pluralism.** Moyer: CLA advocates cite Bernstein's blacksmiths, but "not a lot of us are working with blacksmiths". Theories are tools, chosen by athlete and task ([[principle--motor-control-theory-pluralism-sprint]] [contested], lesson 10).

- **Rehab-specific evidence is case-level.** Differential learning after ACL reconstruction rests on one 18-year-old basketball player. The authors themselves call for larger controlled studies (Arede et al. 2025 [Zotero: 2MPW3ZQ3, PDF p. 1]). Singh et al. (2021) on attentional focus after ACLR is a Level 5 commentary [Zotero: EYKZD68B, PDF p. 1].

- **Load risk.** Inference: "chaotic" drills are hard to dose, and an opposed drill can become an unplanned spike. That is why Taberner pairs the continuum with running-load targets (2022, PDF p. 1). It is also why the course's lesson 6 is about putting constraint changes into the reverse calendar.

I wrote the primer and committed it on step1-triage in two commits (eae21b4, then 8c16789 for citation fixes). Nothing was pushed. It runs about 2,790 words, over the 2,500 target, mostly because of inline citations.

**File:** `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\docs\primers\constraints-led-approach.md`

**Sources used:**
- **Zotero:** 11 papers read at page level (7M8YQMKU, CA2CRR6Z, XZ8KI5V7, WENT2642, T4HB866Z, CBJGJQX5, 2MPW3ZQ3, EYKZD68B, SK32YKG2, G5X9J23E, BJMBTJ8L). Davids 2008, Renshaw 2019 and Chua 2021 are there as records only, with no full text.
- **Vault:** about 17 entries: 12 from Myszka, 2 from Harries, 3 from Moyer.
- **External:** 1, the Bobrownicki critique's abstract.
- **Not read, cited second-hand:** Bernstein, McKay 2024, Choo 2024.
- The Zotero tool rated coverage "thin" only because none of the papers are about collegiate athletes. The library actually covers CLA well.

**Strongest evidence:**
- Young 2015: physical qualities explained 56.7% of the variance in pre-planned change-of-direction speed but only 14.2% in reactive agility. So the Evaluation-phase tests in the rehab templates (10-yard sprint, 5-10-5) certify speed, not agility.
- Winkelman 2017: external cues beat internal cues in collegiate soccer players but made no difference in experienced sprinters.

**Weakest evidence:** No CLA trial exists in collegiate football or return to play. The main supporting study (Lee 2014) is 24 ten-year-old girls learning a tennis forehand. The ACL differential-learning study is one athlete. Singh 2021 is a level-5 commentary.

**RTP course:** Eric is the course's sponsor. Joe Smith is the learner, and every "ask the agent" in Joe's package becomes "ask Eric". The primer frames the gap that way.
- Two of eight lessons are built.
- There's no sign Joe has done the lesson 0001 field task.
- Gray 2015 has only been read as an abstract.
- Bobrownicki, the anchor for lesson 8, isn't in Zotero.
- The Myszka PDF that `_book.md` and the course's CLAUDE.md place in `sources/` isn't there.
